text:
Heavy rain and high winds battered the US west coast, temporarily grounding planes at San Francisco’s airport, flooding roads in Napa county and forcing evacuations in southern California.
The fierce storm, called an atmospheric river, moved from north to south across the state. On Wednesday, San Francisco broke a rain record previously set in 1917. The city’s fire department responded to hundreds of calls, many of which related to flooding, along with downed trees and electrical wires. Flights at San Francisco airport were delayed hours because of wind.
Areas along the city’s Embarcadero were flooded as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm.
Tens of thousands of households lost power across the region.
Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in nearby Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties. South of San Francisco, a 47-mile (76km) segment of Highway 1 near Big Sur was closed on Wednesday for similar reasons.
In southern California, authorities issued evacuation orders as the storm moved south. The Los Angeles county fire department urged residents in the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas to leave, warning of a risk of debris flows.
And in the mountains, heavy snows forced the closure of highways in the Tahoe area. Snow accumulations of up to 4ft (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada.
Atmospheric rivers, huge currents of water vapor that can carry as much or even more water than an actual river, have been growing stronger and deadlier in recent years. In the relatively dry western US, atmospheric river storms provide both essential precipitation and flood risk.
The Golden state is bracing for more weather challenges in the week ahead, when fresh rain is set to coincide with high tides.
